answer:
The head of NASA (the Administrator) during Apollo 11 was **Thomas O. Paine** (often referred to as Tom Paine).

The Apollo 11 mission took place in July 1969, and Paine served as NASA Administrator from October 8, 1968, through March 21, 1969 (when he became acting), and then officially on March 21, 1969, until September 15, 1970. So he was the head of the agency during the historic moon landing on July 20-21, 1969.

Following the Apollo 11 Moon landing in July 1969, many management changes took place at NASA as the agency transitioned to new challenges. Positions including the Apollo Program Director at Headquarters, Director of Launch Operations at [NASA's Kennedy Space Center](https://www.facebook.com/NASAKennedy?__cft__[0]=AZiII4cG6amKRlNNR_3xpj9Sq9lKKzWtl6BupRpzMQrRxOPKGSHkDyqDT-zjnyodrKMo27dpZJk8pmYwnJq0uYWomAr7jgSDr3Bza0-nF9ov1v7F5VW2Y85xgJd8pbFyTcSDlTg78EMxDgtLLPcuykfQLngLOlan&__tn__=-]K-R), Director and Deputy Director of the Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center changed hands. On December 3, NASA Administrator Thomas Paine swore in George Low as the Deputy Administrator of the Agency. Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight, George Mueller, resigned from NASA to return to the private sector, and was succeeded by Dale Myers.

Daniel Goldin held the post for the longest term (nearly 10 years), and is best known for pioneering the ["faster, better, cheaper" approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%22Faster,_better,_cheaper%22_approach "\"Faster, better, cheaper\" approach") to space programs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-goldin_biography-11)
The current administrator is entrepreneur and philanthropist Jared Isaacman, who was nominated by President Donald Trump on November 5, 2025.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-12) He replaced Sean Duffy, who served as acting administrator from July 9, 2025 to December 17, 2025.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-13)Jared Isaacman was nominated by Trump (while he was president-elect) on December 4, 2024,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-:0-14) but his nomination was withdrawn on May 31,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-15) reportedly because of his connections to Elon Musk and donations towards Democratic, anti-Trump politicians.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-16)

Manned Space History:
56 years ago today in 1969, Dr. George M. Low was sworn in as NASA Deputy Administrator by Dr. Thomas 0. Paine, NASA Administrator who had been Deputy Administrator.
The 43-year-old Low was by then a veteran of NASA's Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo manned flight programs. President RIchard Nixon had nominated Low for the post on November 13, 1969, and the Senate confirmed him on November 26, 1969.
Low, who joined the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NASA's predecessor agency) in 1949, was the fourth person to hold the Deputy Administrator post at NASA. He is shown taking the oath of office in the NASA image below.

Manned Space History:
56 years ago today in 1969, Dr. George M. Low was sworn in as NASA Deputy Administrator by Dr. Thomas 0. Paine, NASA Administrator who had been Deputy Administrator.
The 43-year-old Low was by then a veteran of NASA's Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo manned flight programs. President RIchard Nixon had nominated Low for the post on November 13, 1969, and the Senate confirmed him on November 26, 1969.
Low, who joined the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NASA's predecessor agency) in 1949, was the fourth person to hold the Deputy Administrator post at NASA. He is shown taking the oath of office in the NASA image below.

[December 3, 2019](https://www.facebook.com/NASAJSC/posts/pfbid0bJNT2KiHFMPtyCzmxARw9wvjQzadrPrnUoKcUjTq6SroQvVWsVBVFezPDQMirq5el?__cft__[0]=AZiII4cG6amKRlNNR_3xpj9Sq9lKKzWtl6BupRpzMQrRxOPKGSHkDyqDT-zjnyodrKMo27dpZJk8pmYwnJq0uYWomAr7jgSDr3Bza0-nF9ov1v7F5VW2Y85xgJd8pbFyTcSDlTg78EMxDgtLLPcuykfQLngLOlan&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
Following the Apollo 11 Moon landing in July 1969, many management changes took place at NASA as the agency transitioned to new challenges. Positions including the Apollo Program Director at Headquarters, Director of Launch Operations at [NASA's Kennedy Space Center](https://www.facebook.com/NASAKennedy?__cft__[0]=AZiII4cG6amKRlNNR_3xpj9Sq9lKKzWtl6BupRpzMQrRxOPKGSHkDyqDT-zjnyodrKMo27dpZJk8pmYwnJq0uYWomAr7jgSDr3Bza0-nF9ov1v7F5VW2Y85xgJd8pbFyTcSDlTg78EMxDgtLLPcuykfQLngLOlan&__tn__=-]K-R), Director and Deputy Director of the Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center changed hands. On December 3, NASA Administrator Thomas Paine swore in George Low as the Deputy Administrator of the Agency. Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight, George Mueller, resigned from NASA to return to the private sector, and was succeeded by Dale Myers.

## Duties and responsibilities
Daniel Goldin held the post for the longest term (nearly 10 years), and is best known for pioneering the ["faster, better, cheaper" approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%22Faster,_better,_cheaper%22_approach "\"Faster, better, cheaper\" approach") to space programs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-goldin_biography-11)
The current administrator is entrepreneur and philanthropist Jared Isaacman, who was nominated by President Donald Trump on November 5, 2025.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-12) He replaced Sean Duffy, who served as acting administrator from July 9, 2025 to December 17, 2025.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-13)Jared Isaacman was nominated by Trump (while he was president-elect) on December 4, 2024,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-:0-14) but his nomination was withdrawn on May 31,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-15) reportedly because of his connections to Elon Musk and donations towards Democratic, anti-Trump politicians.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_NASA#cite_note-16)

Following the Apollo 11 Moon landing in July 1969, many management changes took place at NASA as the agency transitioned to new challenges. Positions including the Apollo Program Director at Headquarters, Director of Launch Operations at [NASA's Kennedy Space Center](https://www.facebook.com/NASAKennedy?__cft__[0]=AZiII4cG6amKRlNNR_3xpj9Sq9lKKzWtl6BupRpzMQrRxOPKGSHkDyqDT-zjnyodrKMo27dpZJk8pmYwnJq0uYWomAr7jgSDr3Bza0-nF9ov1v7F5VW2Y85xgJd8pbFyTcSDlTg78EMxDgtLLPcuykfQLngLOlan&__tn__=-]K-R), Director and Deputy Director of the Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center changed hands. On December 3, NASA Administrator Thomas Paine swore in George Low as the Deputy Administrator of the Agency. Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight, George Mueller, resigned from NASA to return to the private sector, and was succeeded by Dale Myers.

The head of NASA (the Administrator) during Apollo 11 was **Thomas O. Paine** (often referred to as Tom Paine).

The Apollo 11 mission took place in July 1969, and Paine served as NASA Administrator from October 8, 1968, through March 21, 1969 (when he became acting), and then officially on March 21, 1969, until September 15, 1970. So he was the head of the agency during the historic moon landing on July 20-21, 1969.
